result.topic_en: This page from the editorial summary of Euler's variational-calculus work explains how Euler reduced isoperimetric problems to finding a curve that maximizes or minimizes an integral ∫V dx, notes that the Bernoulli solutions covered only first-order cases, and says Euler found his own geometric method insufficiently natural and wished to recast it as pure analysis.

items.english: All questions of this kind come down to finding a curve, expressed by an equation between the coordinates x and y, for which an integral formula ∫V dx, with V given in any way through x and y, attains a maximum or minimum value.

items.english: The Bernoulli solutions are found to be restricted only to those cases in which the quantity V involves differentials of the first degree alone.

items.english: Our Author has most happily remedied this defect, both in these Commentarii and in a separate work published on this subject, so that hardly anything further remains to be desired.
